solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Shallow watercourse, very warm in continent's extremes

indicators.note: one piece sits in another, enclosed between its letters
extremes are the two ends of a word, so only its outermost letters are kept

parts.note: first and last letters of continent

explanation.surface: A geography note about a shallow stream that runs hot at both ends of a continent.
explanation.walkthrough: A chott is a shallow salt lake or marsh of North Africa, dry in summer.
explanation.definitionFit: A chott is a seasonal salt lake in the Sahara region, fed by shallow water that comes and goes.

clue.text: Sacred charm crafted from a rich nugget, half lost

indicators.note: something crafted is made up afresh, so the letters are worked into a new order
losing half of a word means cutting it down to only its first half

parts.note: taken as written, before the cut

explanation.surface: A holy amulet fashioned out of a gold nugget, with half the nugget gone.
explanation.walkthrough: Halving NUGGET leaves NUG, which joins A RICH as the anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A churinga is an Aboriginal Australian sacred object, a carved stone or wooden talisman.

clue.text: Maize porridge, plain, for consuming at home

indicators.note: a word that consumes another swallows it whole, holding it inside

explanation.surface: Simple maize porridge is the sort of plain food one eats at home.
explanation.walkthrough: Homy, a variant of homey, means homely; in American usage homely means plain.
explanation.definitionFit: Hominy is hulled maize, boiled as a porridge or grits in the American South.

clue.text: Content of storeroom for performer in ring

indicators.note: the content of a word is what lies inside it, so the letters are found within

explanation.surface: The contents of a storeroom kept for a circus performer.
explanation.walkthrough: The ring is a bullring, not a circus ring.
explanation.definitionFit: A torero is a bullfighter on foot, who performs in the bullring.

clue.text: Opening in a college (Oxford) coming up? Not on

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming up means reading from bottom to top
not on tells the solver to strip the letters o and n from the word

parts.note: Merton is a college of Oxford University

explanation.surface: Asking about a vacancy at an Oxford college that may be coming up.
explanation.walkthrough: MERTON loses its ON, A goes in front, and the whole is read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A trema is a small orifice or perforation in anatomy and botany, a technical term for an opening.

clue.text: Essential part of Trinity, one routine seen amid shimmering spires

indicators.note: something shimmering wavers and shifts, so these letters are rearranged
one piece seen amid another lies in its middle

parts.note: these letters reshuffled, split around the middle
a chore is a routine task

explanation.surface: A church scene: shimmering spires and routine worship at the heart of Trinity.
explanation.definitionFit: Perichoresis is the theological doctrine of the mutual indwelling of the three persons of the Trinity.

clue.text: I've affinity for negative charges and rile the police awfully? Not I

indicators.note: done awfully means done badly and in a jumble, so the letters are disordered
not I tells the solver to drop one letter i from the fodder

explanation.surface: Someone drawn to negative charges who riles the police, perhaps a habitual offender.
explanation.walkthrough: Charges here are electrical, not criminal; one I is removed before the letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: An electrophile is a chemical species that seeks electrons, attracted to negatively charged sites.

clue.text: Lives with little to go round, requiring support

indicators.note: one piece going round another wraps it, enclosing it inside

parts.note: a jot is a very little amount

explanation.surface: Someone living on very little who needs support from others.
explanation.definitionFit: A joist is a horizontal beam that supports a floor or ceiling.

clue.text: Cane yielding alternative to honey and source thereof

parts.note: jam is the other spread for bread
the bee is the source of honey

explanation.surface: A breakfast picture: something that yields a substitute for honey and the creature that makes honey.
explanation.definitionFit: A jambee is a light cane or walking stick, an old term from the East Indies trade.

clue.text: Given to faddish theory, I mostly relish accepting upsurge of it

indicators.note: a word accepting another takes it in, holding it between its letters
mostly means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: a smack is a taste or relish

indicators.note: an upsurge rises, and in a down clue that reads the word from bottom to top

explanation.surface: A trend-chaser admits relishing every surge of the latest craze.
explanation.walkthrough: SMACK loses its last letter to SMAC, which holds IT reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: Ismatic describes someone given to isms, following one fashionable doctrine after another.

clue.text: Rotting snake found on island

parts.note: a seps is a serpent of legend, also a skink

explanation.surface: A decaying snake turns up on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: SEPS is a Chambers word for a venomous snake of classical legend.
explanation.definitionFit: Sepsis is putrefaction, the condition of decay caused by bacteria; the noun stands for rotting as a process.

clue.text: Two pairs from Towcester's line-up rarely thrown

indicators.note: two pairs are four letters in total, taken in twos from the word

parts.note: the first two letters and the two after the c, e

explanation.surface: Pairs of jockeys from Towcester racecourse's line-up are rarely thrown.
explanation.walkthrough: Towcester is a Northamptonshire market town with a racecourse; TO and ST are two pairs of letters from its name.
explanation.definitionFit: Tost is an archaic past participle of toss, and something tossed has been thrown; rarely flags the old form.

clue.text: Reptilian creature offering extra drinks after moderation

parts.note: ho is an old word for a halt or limit, moderation

explanation.surface: A creature offering extra drinks after a period of restraint.
explanation.walkthrough: Ho (also spelt whoa) is an old Chambers word for a stop or limit, hence moderation.
explanation.definitionFit: Homorelaps is a genus of small venomous snakes of southern Africa, the harlequin snakes.

clue.text: Beer mixed with rum in part of old helmet

indicators.note: drinks mixed together are blended up, so these letters are combined in a new order

explanation.surface: A beer and rum cocktail served in an old helmet.
explanation.definitionFit: Umbrere is an old Spenserian term for the visor of a helmet, the part shading the face.

clue.text: Swellings, start of plague? What often precedes the word going round

indicators.note: one piece going round another wraps around it, enclosing it

parts.note: from the saying mum's the word

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, which is all that is kept

explanation.surface: Someone noticing swellings and fearing the onset of plague, with gossip going round.
explanation.walkthrough: Mum's the word is an idiom meaning keep quiet; MUM'S wraps the P.
explanation.definitionFit: Mumps is a viral disease named for the swellings of the salivary glands it causes.

clue.text: River that is containing strong current

indicators.note: one piece containing another holds it inside its letters

parts.note: i.e. stands for id est, that is
f is forte, the musical direction for loud and strong

explanation.surface: A river described as having a strong current.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' looks like part of the river picture, but it is the definition, in its sense of prevalent.
explanation.definitionFit: Something rife is widespread and prevalent, as a current rumour is going round now.

clue.text: Midriff showing loss but no sign of age

indicators.note: no sign of something means it has gone, so those letters are removed

explanation.surface: A trim midriff with no sign of age showing.
explanation.walkthrough: WAST is an obsolete spelling of waist.
explanation.definitionFit: The waist, spelt wast in older texts, is the narrow middle of the body around the midriff.

clue.text: Direct fan for repair — it's broken

indicators.note: something sent for repair is taken apart and put together again, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Instructions to send a fan for repair because it's broken.
explanation.definitionFit: Infracted is an old word for broken or fractured, from Latin infringere.

clue.text: Being so gauche shuns set

indicators.note: gauche means clumsy and awkward, so the letters are handled clumsily and jumbled

explanation.surface: Being so socially awkward means one shuns the fashionable set.
explanation.definitionFit: Thusness is the state of being thus, the quality of being so; a jocular noun.

clue.text: Plays subtly dividing feet — near-miss space-wise?

indicators.note: done subtly means done with cunning twists, so the letters are reordered
a piece dividing another goes inside it, splitting it in two

explanation.surface: A dancer subtly plays between feet, a near-miss in spatial terms.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is cryptic: aircraft in a flypast pass close by overhead, nearly but not quite hitting the viewer.
explanation.definitionFit: A flypast is a ceremonial flight of aircraft over a place, passing near in the sky.

clue.text: Ill-natured female retaining right to desire

indicators.note: a word retaining another keeps it held inside

explanation.surface: A bad-tempered woman holding on to her right to want things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ill-natured female' suggests a shrew, which is a trap: the definition is only 'Ill-natured'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrewish means bad-tempered and nagging, like a shrew.

clue.text: Like richly decorated chairs? I left pair in keep of one much admired

indicators.note: something in the keep of another is held in its custody, so it goes inside

explanation.surface: An heirloom chair-owner left a pair of chairs in the care of an admirer.
explanation.definitionFit: Giltwood is carved wood covered with gilding, used in ornate furniture such as chairs; the question mark marks the example.

clue.text: Whitebait substitute causing bad angina

indicators.note: bad here means faulty and disordered, so the word is rearranged

explanation.surface: A dietary warning: switching to whitebait gives someone bad angina.
explanation.definitionFit: Inanga is a small New Zealand fish whose young are eaten as whitebait in place of the European kind.

clue.text: Shot after victory? That's bleak

parts.note: a try is an attempt, a shot

explanation.surface: A sports fan sighs at a shot after a victory: things look bleak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' puts the shot behind the victory.
explanation.definitionFit: Wintry weather or prospects are cold and cheerless, so bleak.

clue.text: Company circulates just like at home in old dance hall

indicators.note: to circulate is to go around, so this piece surrounds the others

explanation.surface: Guests mingle just as if at home in an old dance hall.
explanation.walkthrough: Casino once meant a public room for dancing and music, before it meant gambling house.
explanation.definitionFit: A casino was originally a public building for social gatherings, music and dancing.

clue.text: What examiners do in university encapsulated by 'dark blue'

indicators.note: something encapsulated by another is enclosed within it like a capsule

parts.note: perse is a dark greyish-blue colour

explanation.surface: Exam markers at a university wrapped in Oxford's dark blue colours.
explanation.walkthrough: Dark Blue suggests Oxford University, but here it is the colour perse.
explanation.definitionFit: Examiners read through papers carefully, which is what peruse means.

clue.text: Hurricanes? Real pains when flying about

indicators.note: letters flying about scatter in all directions, so they land in a new order

explanation.surface: Storms causing real pain to people travelling.
explanation.walkthrough: Hurricanes look like storms, but the Hawker Hurricane was a Second World War fighter plane.
explanation.definitionFit: Hurricanes were British fighter aircraft, examples of airplanes, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Idle year requiring cash, commonly

parts.note: to loll is to idle about

explanation.surface: A year off doing nothing still needs money.
explanation.walkthrough: Lolly is British slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: Lolly is an informal British word for money, which the clue's commonly signals as slang.

clue.text: Type of binding always backing pages

indicators.note: backing means moving backwards, so the word reads from right to left

parts.note: ay (aye) is an old word for always

explanation.surface: A bookbinder's style that always has pages at the back.
explanation.definitionFit: Yapp is a style of limp leather bookbinding with overlapping edges, named after a London bookseller.

clue.text: E.g. McEwan's best, badly needed after end of austerity

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, which alone is kept

explanation.surface: A pint of good Scottish beer is badly needed after a spell of austerity.
explanation.walkthrough: McEwan's is an Edinburgh brewery; yill is the Scots word for ale.
explanation.definitionFit: Yill is Scots for ale, and McEwan's best is a Scottish ale, an example of it.

clue.text: What Troon gatecrashers do, showing contempt when shunned by clubs

indicators.note: something shunned is kept out, so that letter is removed from the word

parts.note: to scorn is to show contempt

explanation.surface: Gatecrashers at the Troon golf club scorned by the members.
explanation.walkthrough: Troon is a Scottish golf town, pointing to a Scots word; to sorn is to sponge on others' hospitality.
explanation.definitionFit: Sorn is Scots for imposing oneself on others for food and lodging, as uninvited guests do.

clue.text: Trendy gym accepting one that's unfit

indicators.note: a word accepting another takes it in, between its letters

explanation.surface: A fashionable gym that lets in a member who is out of shape.
explanation.definitionFit: Inapt means unsuitable or not fitting the purpose, so unfit.

clue.text: Liquidised? Such dry fruit did when pounded

indicators.note: something pounded is crushed and mixed, so the letters are reshuffled

parts.note: taken as written; these letters come out of the mix

explanation.surface: Asking if a dry fruit was liquidised when it was pounded.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: the answer plus DID, pounded together, make LIQUIDISED.
explanation.definitionFit: A silique is the long dry seed pod of plants in the cabbage family.

clue.text: After silence, brook head causing the opposite thereof?

parts.note: sh is a call for silence
a rill is a small brook

explanation.surface: A babbling stream breaks the silence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After silence' puts SH first; the definition points back to silence, whose opposite is a loud piercing quality.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrillness is high-pitched piercing noise, the reverse of quiet.

clue.text: Turner cut short yard of wood strip

indicators.note: a word cut short loses its final letter

explanation.surface: A painter like Turner trimming a yard of wooden strip.
explanation.walkthrough: Turner suggests the painter, but it is a lathe, which turns wood.
explanation.definitionFit: Lathy means like a lath, thin as a narrow strip of wood.

clue.text: Combines one agreement incorporating another

indicators.note: a word incorporating another takes it into its body

parts.note: yes is a word of agreement
OK is another word of agreement

explanation.surface: Merging two agreements, one folded into the other, like corporate deals.
explanation.definitionFit: To yoke is to join together, as oxen are coupled under one yoke, so it means combines.
